title: UNIT 2: TWO-DIMENSIONAL MOTION
notes:
✓ Two-dimensional motion → Motion in a plane where position, velocity and acceleration may have both horizontal and vertical components.

◆ Examples → Projectile motion, circular/rotational motion and planetary motion.

✓ Kinematics → Describes motion without considering its causes.

title: 2.1 PROJECTILE MOTION
notes:
✓ Projectile → An object thrown, fired or released that moves mainly under gravity after projection.

◆ Examples → A kicked ball, bullet, javelin and water leaving a hose.

✓ The motion can be separated into horizontal and vertical components.

✓ Horizontal motion → Has zero acceleration when air resistance is ignored, so horizontal velocity remains constant.

✓ Vertical motion → Has constant downward acceleration g ≈ 9.8 m/s².

✓ The combination of the two motions produces a curved/parabolic path.

◆ HORIZONTAL PROJECTILE
For an object projected horizontally:
Vₓ = V₀
x = V₀t
vᵧ = gt
y = ½gt²

◆ INCLINED PROJECTILE
For initial speed V₀ at angle θ:
V₀ₓ = V₀cosθ
V₀ᵧ = V₀sinθ

✓ Horizontal displacement:
x = V₀cosθ · t

✓ Vertical displacement:
y = V₀sinθ · t − ½gt²

✓ Vertical velocity:
vᵧ = V₀sinθ − gt

✓ Maximum height:
H = V₀²sin²θ / 2g

✓ Time of flight:
T = 2V₀sinθ / g

✓ Range:
R = V₀²sin2θ / g

✓ At maximum height, vertical velocity becomes zero but horizontal velocity remains unchanged.

✓ For the same launch and landing level, maximum range occurs at 45°.

title: 2.2 ROTATIONAL MOTION
notes:
✓ Rotational motion → Occurs when a rigid object rotates about a fixed axis.

◆ Examples → A rotating wheel, ceiling fan, flywheel and Earth rotating about its axis.

✓ Rigid body → An object whose shape and distances between its particles remain constant.

◆ ANGULAR DISPLACEMENT (Δθ)
✓ Measures how much an object rotates from its initial to final angular position.

✓ 1 revolution = 2π rad = 360°

◆ ANGULAR VELOCITY (ω)
✓ Rate of change of angular displacement:
ω = Δθ/Δt

✓ It describes how quickly an object rotates.

◆ ANGULAR ACCELERATION (α)
✓ Rate of change of angular velocity:
α = Δω/Δt

✓ It describes how quickly rotational speed changes.

◆ CONNECTION WITH LINEAR MOTION
✓ s = rθ
✓ v = rω
✓ at = rα

◆ CONSTANT ANGULAR ACCELERATION
✓ ωf = ω₀ + αt
✓ Δθ = ω₀t + ½αt²
✓ ωf² = ω₀² + 2αΔθ
✓ Δθ = ½(ω₀ + ωf)t

✓ Points farther from the axis travel a greater distance and have greater linear speed, even though all points of a rigid body have the same angular velocity.

title: 2.3 ROTATIONAL DYNAMICS
notes:
✓ Rotational dynamics → Studies the causes of rotational motion.

✓ Just as force changes linear motion, torque changes rotational motion.

◆ TORQUE (τ)
✓ Torque → The turning effect of a force about an axis.

✓ τ = rFsinθ

✓ A larger force, longer lever arm or more suitable angle produces greater torque.

✓ Maximum torque occurs when the force is perpendicular to the radius (θ = 90°).

◆ MOMENT OF INERTIA (I)
✓ Moment of inertia → The rotational equivalent of mass. It measures how strongly an object resists changes in its rotational motion.

✓ For a point mass:
I = mr²

✓ For several particles:
I = Σmr²

✓ Its value depends on both the amount of mass and how far the mass is distributed from the axis.

◆ NEWTON’S SECOND LAW FOR ROTATION
✓ τnet = Iα

✓ Thus, for the same torque, a larger moment of inertia produces a smaller angular acceleration.

◆ LINEAR ↔ ROTATIONAL
✓ Force F ↔ Torque τ
✓ Mass m ↔ Moment of inertia I
✓ Acceleration a ↔ Angular acceleration α

✓ Torque is the cause of angular acceleration in the same way that force is the cause of linear acceleration.

title: 2.4 PLANETARY MOTION AND KEPLER’S LAWS
notes:
✓ Planetary motion → Describes the movement of planets around the Sun.

✓ Kepler developed three laws from observations of planetary motion.

✓ Newton later explained these laws using gravity and his laws of motion.

◆ HELIOCENTRIC MODEL
✓ The Sun is at the center of the planetary system and planets revolve around it.

◆ GEOCENTRIC MODEL
✓ The Earth is considered the center, with the Sun and other celestial bodies moving around it.

◆ KEPLER’S FIRST LAW — LAW OF ORBITS
✓ Planets move in elliptical orbits with the Sun at one focus.

◆ KEPLER’S SECOND LAW — LAW OF AREAS
✓ The line joining a planet to the Sun sweeps out equal areas in equal time intervals.

✓ Therefore:
Planet moves faster when closer to the Sun.
Planet moves slower when farther from the Sun.

◆ KEPLER’S THIRD LAW — LAW OF PERIODS
✓ The square of the orbital period is proportional to the cube of the average orbital radius:

T² ∝ R³

✓ Therefore:
T₁²/T₂² = R₁³/R₂³

✓ A planet farther from the Sun takes a longer time to complete one orbit.

✓ Kepler’s laws also help describe the motion of moons and artificial satellites.

title: 2.5 NEWTON’S LAW OF UNIVERSAL GRAVITATION
notes:
✓ Newton’s law of universal gravitation → Every mass attracts every other mass with a gravitational force.

✓ This force acts along the line joining their centers.

◆ GRAVITATIONAL FORCE
✓ F = Gm₁m₂/r²

◆ Where:
G → Universal gravitational constant
m₁, m₂ → Interacting masses
r → Distance between their centers

✓ The force:
Increases when either mass increases.
Decreases as the square of distance increases.
Is always attractive.

◆ ACCELERATION DUE TO GRAVITY
✓ For a body of mass M:
g = GM/r²

✓ Near Earth's surface:
g ≈ 9.8 m/s²

◆ GRAVITY AND ORBITAL MOTION
✓ Gravity provides the centripetal force required for planets and satellites to remain in orbit.

✓ Newton’s gravitational law therefore provides the physical explanation for Kepler’s laws.

✓ Greater distance from a massive body → weaker gravitational attraction.

✓ The same law applies to objects on Earth, planets around the Sun, moons around planets and artificial satellites.
